rules:
OUTPUT FRAMING: stdout is always `yaml.dump(...)` plus one extra newline from print(). yaml.dump itself always ends with exactly one '
', so successful stdout always ends with '

'.

EXPLICIT DOCUMENT END: an extra line containing exactly '...' is appended when, and only when, the root node is emitted as a PLAIN scalar (int, float, bool, null, timestamp, and strings that need no quoting). It is NOT emitted for quoted scalars ('5', '', "h\xE9llo"), for literal/folded block scalars (!!binary |), for block collections, or for flow collections ([] / {} / !!set {}). So `x` -> 'x
...

'; `!!str 5` -> "'5'

".

DUMP DEFAULTS: default_flow_style=False (block style for non-empty collections; empty list -> '[]', empty dict -> '{}'), indent=2, allow_unicode=False (non-ASCII escaped as \xNN/\uNNNN inside double quotes), no '---' start marker, no %YAML/%TAG directives ever emitted, mapping keys sorted when mutually comparable.

SAFE TAG WHITELIST (tag:yaml.org,2002:X): str, int, float, bool, null, binary, timestamp, seq, map, set, pairs, omap. Everything else under that prefix (including merge, value, yaml, and all python/*) fails with ConstructorError: "could not determine a constructor for the tag '<full-tag>'". Any local tag (!foo) fails the same way with the tag shown as '!foo'.

'!!X' shorthand expands to 'tag:yaml.org,2002:X'; the error message always shows the fully expanded URI. '!X' stays '!X'. Verbatim '!<URI>' uses URI literally (so '!<tag:yaml.org,2002:str>' == '!!str'; '!<!foo>' == '!foo'; '!<x>' yields tag 'x' which is unknown -> ConstructorError).

Bare '!' (non-specific tag) does NOT force !!str: it falls back to normal implicit resolution. '! 5' -> 5 (int, output '5
...

'); '! [1,2]' -> seq; '! {a: 1}' -> map.

'!!' with nothing after it, and '!<>' , are scanner errors: yaml.scanner.ScannerError: 'while parsing a tag' / 'expected URI, but found <c>' with two context blocks. Percent-escapes in tags are URL-decoded before lookup ('!foo%20bar' -> tag '!foo bar', '!!str%20' -> 'tag:yaml.org,2002:str ').

%TAG directives are honored for the document that follows: '%TAG !e! tag:yaml.org,2002:' makes '!e!str' == '!!str'. '%TAG ! !local-' makes '!thing' == '!local-thing'. A handle used without a preceding %TAG (or with the %TAG after the node) -> yaml.parser.ParserError: 'while parsing a node' / "found undefined tag handle '!e!'".

!!str: takes the scalar text verbatim. Applied to a non-scalar -> ConstructorError 'expected a scalar node, but found sequence|mapping'. Dumping a string re-quotes per normal string rules, so '!!str 5' -> "'5'", '!!str null' -> "'null'", '!!str yes' -> "'yes'", '!!str "@x"' -> "'@x'".

!!int parsing (YAML 1.1 style, on the raw scalar text): strip '_'; optional leading sign; '0' -> 0; '0x'/'0X' prefix -> base 16; '0b' -> base 2; '0o' or a bare leading '0' followed by digits -> base 8; contains ':' -> sexagesimal (sum of base-60 digits, sign applied); otherwise int(text) (which tolerates surrounding whitespace). Arbitrary precision (bigints).

!!int failure modes: empty scalar -> IndexError: string index out of range (uncaught, rc=1). Whitespace-only or otherwise unparseable -> ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '<text>'. '!!int 5.5' is a ValueError, not a truncation. These are raw Python exceptions, not ConstructorError.

!!float parsing: strip '_'; lowercase; '.inf'/'+.inf' -> Infinity, '-.inf' -> -Infinity, '.nan' -> NaN; contains ':' -> sexagesimal as float; otherwise float(text) (accepts leading/trailing spaces, exponents; rejects hex). Overflow ('1e400') becomes Infinity, not an error. Empty scalar -> IndexError: string index out of range; unparseable -> ValueError: could not convert string to float: '<text>'.
Float dump formatting: integral values get '.0' ('!!float 1' -> '1.0'), -0.0 stays '-0.0', Infinity -> '.inf', -Infinity -> '-.inf', NaN -> '.nan'.

!!bool: lookup of text.lower() in exactly {yes,no,true,false,on,off}. Anything else (including 'y','n','1','0','') raises a raw KeyError with the LOWERCASED text: KeyError: 'y'. Dumps as 'true'/'false'.

!!null: never fails and completely ignores the scalar content. '!!null ""', '!!null', '!!null null', '!!null x', '!!null "NULL"' all give None -> 'null
...

'.

!!binary load: take scalar text, encode to ASCII (non-ASCII -> ConstructorError: "failed to convert base64 data into ascii: 'ascii' codec can't encode character '\\xNN' in position N: ordinal not in range(128)"), then base64-decode leniently: every character outside the base64 alphabet (spaces, newlines, '-', '_', '!') is silently DISCARDED before decoding; only length/padding errors surface as ConstructorError: 'failed to decode base64 data: Incorrect padding' (or 'Invalid base64-encoded string: ...'). '!!binary "!!!"' and '!!binary "===="' both give empty bytes.

!!binary dump: bytes are re-encoded to standard base64, hard-wrapped at 76 characters per line (RFC2045 / Python base64.encodebytes: 57 input bytes per output line) with a trailing newline, then emitted as a LITERAL block scalar with the explicit tag: '!!binary |' followed by each 76-char chunk indented at parent_indent+2. The 76-char wrap width is independent of nesting depth / emitter width. Empty bytes cannot use a block scalar, so they emit as '!!binary ""'.

!!timestamp load: matched against the YAML 1.1 timestamp regex. Date-only ('2001-12-14', '2001-1-1') -> a date object, dumped as 'YYYY-MM-DD'. With a time part -> a datetime, dumped as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS' (space separator, not 'T'), with '.ffffff' (always exactly 6 digits) only if fractional seconds are non-zero, and '+HH:MM'/'-HH:MM' offset appended if a zone was given ('Z' -> '+00:00'). The offset is preserved, NOT normalized to UTC. Non-matching text -> AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'groupdict' (rc=1).

!!seq / !!map applied to the wrong kind -> ConstructorError: 'expected a sequence node, but found scalar|mapping' / 'expected a mapping node, but found scalar|sequence'. Applied to the right kind, they are no-ops and no tag is emitted on output.

!!set load: requires a mapping node ('!!set [a,b]' -> ConstructorError 'expected a mapping node, but found sequence'); values are discarded (only keys kept, '!!set {a: 1}' == '!!set {a}'); keys must be hashable (a collection key -> ConstructorError 'while constructing a mapping' / 'found unhashable key').

!!set dump: emitted as a block mapping with the explicit '!!set' tag and every value 'null'. At root the tag occupies its own line ('!!set
a: null
b: null
'); nested it goes after the parent indicator ('k: !!set
  a: null'), with entries at parent_indent+2. Empty set -> '!!set {}' (flow, tag inline). Keys are sorted when comparable.

NON-DETERMINISM: a !!set whose members are not all mutually comparable (e.g. mixing int and str) cannot be sorted, so the dumper falls back to Python set iteration order, which varies between runs due to string hash randomization. Mixed-type MAPPINGS are deterministic (sort fails -> source insertion order is kept).

!!omap load: requires a sequence of single-entry mappings; produces a list of 2-element tuples, which dumps as a nested block sequence with NO tag ('- - a\n  - 1'). Errors: non-sequence -> ConstructorError 'while constructing an ordered map\\nexpected a sequence, but found mapping'; non-mapping item -> '...expected a mapping of length 1, but found scalar'; item with 2 entries -> '...expected a single mapping item, but found 2 items'. Empty -> '[]'.

!!pairs behaves identically to !!omap (same shapes, message text 'while constructing pairs' instead of 'while constructing an ordered map') but duplicate keys are preserved since the result is just a list of pairs.

ANCHOR/ALIAS LOAD: '&name node' registers the node; '*name' reuses the SAME object. Undefined alias -> yaml.composer.ComposerError: "found undefined alias 'a'". Re-using an anchor name -> yaml.composer.ComposerError: "found duplicate anchor 'a'; first occurrence <ctx> second occurrence <ctx>". Anchor and tag may appear in either order ('&a !!str 5' and '!!str &a 5' are both fine). '&a' with no node -> null. An anchor immediately followed by an alias ('[&a *a]') is a ParserError: 'while parsing a flow sequence' / "expected ',' or ']', but got '<alias>'".

WHICH VALUES GET RE-ANCHORED ON DUMP: only values whose Python type is aliasable — list, dict, set, datetime.date, datetime.datetime (and non-empty tuples, i.e. !!omap/!!pairs items). NEVER aliased: None, bool, int, float, str, bytes, and the empty tuple. Therefore '[&x abc, *x]' dumps as two plain 'abc' lines with no &/* at all, while '{a: &v [1,2], b: *v}' dumps '&id001'/'*id001'.

ANCHOR NAME GENERATION: names are always 'id%03d' starting at id001 (source anchor names are discarded). Only nodes that are actually referenced more than once get a name. The counter is incremented at the moment a repeated node is encountered for the SECOND time during a depth-first walk of the represented tree (mapping keys already sorted, key visited before value). Consequence: the node whose duplicate is reached first gets id001, even if another shared node appeared earlier in the output. Example: '[[&v1 [1]], &v2 [2], *v2, *v1]' -> the nested [1] prints '&id002' and [2] prints '&id001'.

ANCHOR PLACEMENT: for a non-empty collection the '&idNNN' is written alone on the line where the value would start, and the collection body follows on subsequent lines (block seq items at the PARENT's indent, block map entries at parent+2). At root: '&id001\n- ...' or '&id001\nkey: ...'. For an empty collection or a scalar the anchor is inline: '- &id001 []', 'a: &id001 {}', 'd: &id001 2001-01-01'. Tag and anchor together: anchor first, then tag ('s: &id001 !!set').

RECURSION: self-referential structures load and dump successfully with no error and no recursion limit hit. '&a [*a]' -> '&id001
- *id001

'; '&a {self: *a}' -> '&id001
self: *id001

'. Aliases may be used as mapping keys on output ('*id001: 1').

An alias used as a mapping key is legal if the target is hashable; otherwise ConstructorError 'while constructing a mapping' + 'found unhashable key', where the second context block points at the ANCHOR definition site, not the alias. Duplicate mapping keys (e.g. '&k key' plus '*k') collapse with last-value-wins.

Merge keys ('<<: *base') copy the referenced mapping's values, so nested collections become shared objects and the dumper emits &idNNN/*idNNN for nodes that had no anchor in the source: '{base: &b {x: [1]}, d: {<<: *b}}' -> 'base:
  x: &id001
  - 1
d:
  x: *id001

'.

The last stderr lines are '<ExceptionClass>: <message>' optionally followed by yaml context blocks of the form '  in "<unicode string>", line L, column C:' / '    <source line>' / '    ^', then a final line '[PYI-<varying number>:ERROR] Failed to execute script \'test16\' due to unhandled exception!'. Exception classes observed: yaml.scanner.ScannerError, yaml.parser.ParserError, yaml.composer.ComposerError, yaml.constructor.ConstructorError, ValueError, IndexError, KeyError, AttributeError. A single explicit '--- x' or leading '%YAML 1.1' directive is accepted and produces the same output as the bare node; a trailing '...' in the input is also accepted.

Root-level PLAIN scalars get an extra '...' document-end line but quoted scalars and block scalars do not. So '!!str x' -> 'x
...

' but '!!str 5' -> "'5'

Anchors/aliases from the source are thrown away and regenerated as &id001/*id001 — and the numbering follows the order in which each shared node is encountered the SECOND time in a DFS over the ALREADY-SORTED tree. This means '&id002' can appear textually before '&id001' in the output.
Strings, ints, floats, bools, null and bytes are never re-aliased: '[&x abc, *x]' loses all anchor information and prints the value twice. Only list/dict/set/date/datetime get &/*.
Recursive structures dump fine (no error, no infinite loop) — '&a [*a]' yields '&id001\n- *id001'.
Merge keys can INTRODUCE anchors that were never in the source, because '<<' shares the inner objects by reference.
!!binary silently discards every non-base64 character rather than rejecting it: '!!binary "!!!"' loads as empty bytes and dumps as '!!binary ""'. Only padding-length errors raise.
!!binary output is hard-wrapped at exactly 76 base64 characters per line no matter how deeply indented, so nested lines exceed the usual 80-column emitter width.

Several tag coercion failures leak raw Python exceptions instead of yaml errors: '!!int ""' -> IndexError: string index out of range; '!!bool "y"' -> KeyError: 'y'; '!!timestamp abc' -> AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'groupdict'.

!!null ignores its content entirely — '!!null x' is null, never an error.
A !!set with mixed-type members produces NON-DETERMINISTIC key order across runs (hash randomization); mixed-type mappings are deterministic because the failed sort falls back to insertion order.
!!omap and !!pairs both become plain nested sequences with the tag dropped, so the round trip is lossy: '!!omap [{a: 1}]' -> '- - a\n  - 1'.
!!set keeps its tag and, at document root, prints '!!set' alone on the first line before the entries.
Bare '!' does not coerce to string: '! 5' stays the integer 5.

Date/datetime values ARE aliasable, so '[&t !!timestamp 2001-01-01, *t]' emits '&id001'/'*id001' — unlike every other scalar type.

OUTPUT SHAPE (needed to read all evidence below): for a top-level scalar document stdout is `<dumped scalar>
...

` (yaml.dump emits an explicit `...` document-end line for a bare scalar root, plus print()'s extra newline). For a top-level collection there is no `...`: `[X]` -> `- <X>

`, `{k: X}` -> `k: <X>

`. All probes below use `[VALUE]` so the value's own dumped form is unambiguous.

STR-VS-OTHER DISAMBIGUATION RULE (how to read the evidence, and a required property of the reimplementation): the dumper re-runs the implicit resolver on any plain string it is about to emit; if the plain form would resolve to a non-`str` tag it is emitted single-quoted instead. Therefore in the dump, a bare/unquoted token is either (a) the canonical repr of a resolved non-string type, or (b) a string that the resolver does NOT recognize; a single-quoted token is always a string that WOULD have been mis-resolved. Control: `[!!str 1]` -> `- '1'`, `[!!str true]` -> `- 'true'`, `[!!str 2001-01-01]` -> `- '2001-01-01'`, `[!!str 20011214]` -> `- '20011214'`.

RESOLUTION ORDER: apply the implicit resolvers in this order against the plain scalar's exact (post-parse) text: bool, int, float, timestamp (yaml.org,2002:timestamp), null, merge/value/yaml (`<<`,`=`,`!`,`&`,`*`), and finally fall back to `tag:yaml.org,2002:str`. Practically: try bool -> null -> int -> float -> timestamp -> str; the patterns below are mutually exclusive so order only matters for documentation.

PLAIN SCALAR TEXT PREPARATION happens before resolution: leading/trailing spaces of a plain scalar are stripped and internal line breaks are folded to a single space. `[ yes ]` -> `- true`; `[yes ]` -> `- true`; input `1\n2` (two lines) -> plain scalar "1 2" -> `1 2` (a str, dumped bare). A `#` starts a comment: `yes # comment` -> `true`.

BOOL: resolves to Python bool ONLY for these exact 22 spellings (dumped as `true`/`false`): true True TRUE / false False FALSE / yes Yes YES / no No NO / on On ON / off Off OFF. Note the pattern is all-lower, Capitalized, or all-UPPER only — arbitrary mixed case is a STRING: `yES`,`nO`,`TrUe`,`tRUE`,`fAlse`,`oN`,`oFF`,`OFf`,`YEs`,`TRue` all stay str and dump bare.

BOOL SURPRISE: the single letters `y`, `Y`, `n`, `N` are NOT booleans in this implementation (PyYAML omits them even though YAML 1.1 lists them). `[y]` -> `- y` (str), `[Y]`,`[n]`,`[N]` likewise. Do not treat them as bool.

NULL: resolves to null for the exact spellings `null`, `Null`, `NULL`, `~`, and the EMPTY string. Mixed case (`NuLl`,`nULL`) is a str. `Nil`,`nil`,`None`,`none` are strings. Empty/omitted values: `--a ''` -> `null
...

`; `{k: }` and `{k:}` -> `k: null`; `a:` -> `a: null`; `-` at top level parses as a block sequence with an empty item -> `- null`; `?` at top level -> `null: null`; `#` (comment-only doc) -> `null
...

`.

INT — decimal: `^[-+]?(0|[1-9][0-9_]*)$`. Underscores are removed before parsing and may appear anywhere after the first digit, including trailing/doubled: `1_000`->1000, `1_0_0`->100, `1__0`->10, `1_`->1, `0_`->0. Leading `_` is NOT allowed (`_1` is str). `+1`->1, `-1`->-1, `-0`->0, `+0`->0, `00`->0, `000`->0 (these match the OCTAL branch, see below, and still give 0). Arbitrary precision: `12345678901234567890123456789` and `9223372036854775808` round-trip exactly (BigInt required in JS).
INT — NO `0o` SUPPORT: `0o17` resolves to str (dumps bare as `0o17`), as do `0O17`, `0o`, `0o8`. This is a YAML-1.1 resolver, not 1.2.

INT — sexagesimal: `^[-+]?[1-9][0-9_]*(:[0-5]?[0-9])+$`; value = fold left over the colon-separated parts: acc = acc*60 + part, applying the sign at the end. Each group after a colon is 1 or 2 digits with value 0..59. `1:20`->80, `1:20:30`->4830, `1:2:3`->3723, `1:5`->65, `1:0`->60, `1:59`->119, `59:59`->3599, `190:20:30`->685230, `-1:20:30`->-4830, `+1:20`->80, `1:2:3:4`->223384, `1:20:30:40:50`->17390450, `1_0:20`->620. The FIRST group must start with 1-9: `0:0:0`, `0:20`, `00:20`, `0_1:20` are STRINGS. Groups may not contain `_`: `1:2_0` is a str. Out-of-range groups make it a str: `1:60`, `12:60:00`. Note `1:` and `1:20:` are not scalars at all — inside `[...]` they parse as single-pair flow mappings (`[1:]` -> `- 1: null`).

FLOAT — the resolver regex is a 5-way alternation; anything not matching is not a float:
  (a) `[-+]?[0-9][0-9_]*\.[0-9_]*([eE][-+][0-9]+)?`  (digits, mandatory '.', optional fraction, optional SIGNED exponent)
  (b) `\.[0-9][0-9_]*([eE][-+][0-9]+)?`  (leading dot — NO leading sign permitted)
  (c) `[-+]?[0-9][0-9_]*(:[0-5]?[0-9])+\.[0-9_]*`  (sexagesimal float, mandatory trailing '.')
  (d) `[-+]?\.(inf|Inf|INF)`
  (e) `\.(nan|NaN|NAN)`  (NO sign permitted)

FLOAT SURPRISE 1 — the exponent MUST carry an explicit `+` or `-`. `1.0e-3`->0.001, `1.0E+3`->1000.0, `1.5e+3`->1500.0, `1.5E-3`->0.0015, `0.5e+1`->5.0. But `1.0e5`, `1.5e3`, `.5e3`, `5.e3`, `1_000.5e3`, `1.0e+1_0` are all STRINGS (dumped bare, unchanged).

FLOAT SURPRISE 2 — an exponent with no `.` is never a float: `1e3`, `1E3`, `1e+3`, `1E+3`, `1e-3`, `1e400`, `1e-400`, `5e-324`, `1.7976931348623157e308` are all STRINGS. `1e`, `1.0e`, `1.0e+`, `e5`, `E5`, `.e5`, `1.e5` are STRINGS too (note `1.e5` fails because branch (a) requires the exponent to be signed, and the fraction `[0-9_]*` can't contain `e`).

FLOAT SURPRISE 3 — sign asymmetry on the leading-dot form: `.5`->0.5 float, `.0`->0.0 float, but `+.5` and `-.5` are STRINGS (branch (b) has no sign). Likewise `+.0`, `-.0` are strings. However `-0.5`->-0.5 and `+0.0`->0.0 (branch (a) does allow a sign), and `-0.0`->-0.0 float.

OUTPUT SHAPE: stdout = D + "

THE '...' RULE (exact): after the document body, dump appends the line "...\n" if and only if the ROOT node was emitted as a PLAIN scalar. Equivalently (PyYAML internals): the emitter sets open_ended=true only inside write_plain() when root_context is true, and at stream end it writes "..." + newline if open_ended. Nothing else sets it.

Consequence A: root value is a scalar whose chosen output style is plain -> marker present. This covers: null (printed 'null'), booleans (true/false), ints, floats (including .inf, -.inf, .nan), date / datetime values, and any string that PyYAML considers plain-safe.

Consequence B: NO marker when the root scalar is emitted single-quoted ('...'), double-quoted ("..."), or as a block scalar (|), e.g. !!binary. NO marker when the root is any collection: block mapping, block sequence, empty flow sequence [], empty flow mapping {}, tagged collection (!!set), or a collection carrying a root anchor (&id001 on its own line).
Consequence C: a plain scalar that is NOT at the root never triggers the marker. `[1,2]` ends with the plain scalar 2 yet emits no '...' because root_context is false for children.

A root string is plain (and therefore gets the marker) when: it is non-empty; it contains no line break (\n, \r, \r\n, U+0085 all count as breaks after reader normalization); it contains no character requiring double quoting (tab, C0/C1 controls, non-ASCII since allow_unicode=false, U+2028/U+2029, U+FEFF not at position 0); it has no leading or trailing space; it does not start with any of the indicators - ? : , [ ] { } # & * ! | > ' " % @ ` (note: a leading '-' or '?' or ':' NOT followed by a space is still plain, e.g. -a, ?a, :a are plain); it does not start with the 3-character prefix "---" or "..." (startswith test, so '----' and '...x' are quoted but '--' and 'x...' are plain); it does not contain ": " or " #"; it does not end with ':'; and it does not resolve to a non-str type (so 'null', 'true', 'yes', 'on', '42', '0', '~', '3.14' are quoted -> no marker).

USAGE LINE (exact): `usage: PROG [-h] --a A` followed by a single \n.

HELP TEXT (exact, byte-verified, stdout only, exit 0): `usage: PROG [-h] --a A

options:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit
  --a A
`. Note: section header is `options:` (Python >= 3.10 wording, not `optional arguments:`); two spaces of indent before each option; exactly two spaces between `-h, --help` and `show this...`; the `--a A` line has NO help text after it; there is a blank line between the usage line and `options:`; no trailing blank line beyond the final 
.

-h and --help are identical and are handled EAGERLY during parsing: help is printed to stdout and the process exits 0 immediately, before required-argument checking, before 'expected one argument' errors, and before unrecognized-argument checking. So `--a x --help`, `--help extra`, `-h --a`, `-h x`, `-h -h` all print help and exit 0. Nothing goes to stderr.

LONG-OPTION PREFIX ABBREVIATION IS ENABLED (allow_abbrev default True). Registered long options are exactly `--help` and `--a`. Any unambiguous prefix of a long option is accepted: `--h`, `--he`, `--hel`, `--help` all mean --help; `--a` is an exact match for --a (and is NOT ambiguous with --help). Abbreviations are matched only against long options, and only when the token starts with `--`.

AMBIGUITY: a `--` token whose name part is empty matches all long options. `--=x` -> exit 2, stderr `usage: ...\nPROG: error: ambiguous option: --=x could match --help, --a` — note the candidate list is in registration order (--help first, then --a), comma+space separated, and the offending token is echoed in full including `=x`.
OPTION NAMES ARE CASE-SENSITIVE: `--A`, `--A=x`, `-A` are all unknown. Unknown tokens do not error immediately; they are collected as 'extras'.
There are NO positional arguments. Any non-option token (and any unknown option token) becomes an 'extra'.

ERROR PRECEDENCE: (1) eager -h/--help -> exit 0; (2) per-option value errors during the scan (`expected one argument`, `ignored explicit argument`, `ambiguous option`) -> exit 2; (3) missing required --a -> exit 2; (4) unrecognized/extra arguments -> exit 2. Critically, MISSING --a IS REPORTED BEFORE UNRECOGNIZED EXTRAS: `--b x` yields `the following arguments are required: --a`, NOT `unrecognized arguments: --b x`.

MISSING --a (includes empty argv, `--`, `-- --a x`, `--b x`, `--A x`, `-a x`, `-x`, `-`, `-5`, `@args`, `---a x`, `--ab x`): stdout is EMPTY; stderr is exactly `usage: PROG [-h] --a A\nPROG: error: the following arguments are required: --a\n`; exit code 2.

MISSING VALUE for --a (`--a` last token, `--a --b`, `--a --`, `--a -- x`, `--a -h`, `--a --a`, `--a -x`, `--a -abc`, `--a -1e3`, `--a -1x`, `--a -5.`): stdout EMPTY; stderr exactly `usage: PROG [-h] --a A\nPROG: error: argument --a: expected one argument\n`; exit 2. The error label is `--a` (the single option string), whereas for help it is `-h/--help` (all option strings joined by '/').

VALUES THAT LOOK LIKE OPTIONS: a separate token is rejected as --a's value if it starts with '-' AND is longer than 1 char AND does not match the negative-number regex `^-\d+$|^-\d*\.\d+$`. Accepted: `-5`, `-0`, `-007`, `-5.5`, `-.5`, `-` (bare single dash), and anything not starting with '-' (including ' -x' with a leading space). Rejected (-> 'expected one argument'): `-x`, `-abc`, `-1e3`, `-1x`, `-5.`, `-h`, `--b`, `--`, `--a`. This permissiveness for negative numbers holds because the parser registers no option strings that look like negative numbers.

`--a=VALUE` FORM: split on the FIRST '=' only; everything after it is the raw value, with NO option-looking checks. `--a=-5` -> '-5', `--a=--b` -> '--b', `--a=x=y` -> 'x=y', `--a==x` -> '=x', `--a=` -> '' (empty string). This is the only way to pass an option-looking value.

`--help=x` (or any abbreviation with an explicit value, since --help takes no argument): exit 2, stderr `usage: PROG [-h] --a A\nPROG: error: argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument 'x'\n`. The value is single-quoted with Python repr-style quoting.
REPEATED --a: plain `store` action, so the LAST occurrence wins. `--a x --a y` -> 'y'; `--a x --a=y` -> 'y'. No error, exit 0.

SHORT-FLAG CLUSTERS: `-ha` is parsed as -h plus leftover chars; since -h is an eager zero-arg flag, help is printed and exit is 0 (the trailing 'a' is discarded). `-xh` starts with an unknown short char, so the whole token becomes an extra (-> required-argument error). `-h -h` -> help, exit 0.

`--` SEPARATOR: a bare `--` ends option parsing; everything after it is treated as positional. Because there are no positionals, those tokens become extras. IMPORTANT (version-specific): the `--` token itself is NOT stripped from the extras list — it is echoed back in the unrecognized-arguments message. `--a=y --` -> `unrecognized arguments: --`; `--a=y -- x` -> `unrecognized arguments: -- x`; `--a=y -- --a x` -> `unrecognized arguments: -- --a x`; `--a=y -- --` -> `unrecognized arguments: -- --`. A `--` BEFORE --a hides it: `-- --a x` -> required-argument error. `--` is never consumed as --a's value.

PROG: error: unrecognized arguments: <extras>

surprises: `--b x` does NOT produce 'unrecognized arguments: --b x' — it produces 'the following arguments are required: --a'. argparse checks required actions before reporting extras, so an unknown option combined with a missing required option surfaces only the missing-required error.

`--a -5`, `--a -0`, `--a -007`, `--a -5.5`, `--a -.5` are all ACCEPTED as values, but `--a -1e3`, `--a -5.`, `--a -1x` are REJECTED with 'expected one argument'. The accept/reject line is the regex ^-\d+$|^-\d*\.\d+$, not 'is this a number'.

`--a -` is accepted (a bare single dash is not option-like), and it is valid YAML meaning a one-element block sequence [null], so stdout is `- null\n\n` — no `...` document-end marker, unlike scalar results.

A trailing/leading `--` separator is NOT swallowed: it reappears verbatim in the 'unrecognized arguments' message (`--a=y --` -> `unrecognized arguments: --`). Newer Python argparse versions strip it; this build does not. Reimplementations must echo it.
`--` never provides a value to `--a`: `--a -- x` fails with 'expected one argument' rather than binding 'x'.
`--=x` is an ambiguous-option error listing BOTH long options ('could match --help, --a'), because the empty name before '=' is a prefix of everything.
Prefix abbreviation is on, so `--h`, `--he`, `--hel` all print help — an implementer who only matched exact strings would report these as unknown.
-h/--help is eager and beats every error: `--a x --help extra`, `--help extra`, `-h --a` (missing value!) all exit 0 with help on stdout.
`-ha` exits 0 with help (short cluster: -h consumed, trailing 'a' silently dropped), while `-xh` exits 2 with the missing-required error.
The error label differs per option: '--a' for the string option but '-h/--help' for help ('argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument'). The label is all option strings joined with '/'.

The program name in every message is basename(argv[0]) at runtime, so it changes if the binary is renamed or invoked through a symlink (verified: 'zzz_prog', 'my prog' with an embedded space and no quoting).
COLUMNS affects the usage/help layout (wrapping and continuation indentation) but never wraps the 'PROG: error: ...' line.
An empty-string extra arg yields a message with a dangling space: 'unrecognized arguments: ' followed directly by the newline.

YAML failures exit 1 (not 2) and dump a full Python traceback to stderr, including a PyInstaller-specific final line '[PYI-<varying-number>:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test16' due to unhandled exception!'. `@args` is not file-expansion (fromfile_prefix_chars is unset) — it is just an unknown positional.

FLOAT EMISSION ALGORITHM: given a JS number f: (1) if Number.isNaN(f) emit '.nan'; (2) else if f === +Infinity emit '.inf'; (3) else if f === -Infinity emit '-.inf'; (4) else compute Python repr(f) and lowercase it; then if the text contains 'e' but no '.', insert '.0' before the FIRST 'e' (i.e. replace first 'e' with '.0e'). Emit plain, unquoted.

Python repr(float) semantics you must reproduce exactly: shortest decimal string that round-trips to the same double; always contains a '.' or an exponent (so integral floats get a '.0' suffix: 1.0, 100.0, -0.0, 1000000000000000.0); fixed notation is used when the decimal exponent e satisfies -4 <= e < 16, exponential notation otherwise; exponential form is '<mantissa>e<sign><digits>' with an ALWAYS-present sign and at least 2 exponent digits (zero-padded): 1e+16, 1e-05, 5e-324, 1.2345678901234567e+19, 1e-100 (3 digits, no padding needed).

Concrete float fixed/exponential boundary: 1.0e+15 -> '1000000000000000.0'; 1.0e+16 -> '1.0e+16'; 9999999999999998.0 -> '9999999999999998.0'; 0.0001 -> '0.0001'; 0.00001 -> '1.0e-05'. Note JS Number.prototype.toString() does NOT match (it switches at 1e21 and prints '1e+21' style differently), so a custom repr is required.

The '.0e' fixup only fires when repr has an exponent and no dot. So repr '1e+20' -> '1.0e+20', '5e-324' -> '5.0e-324', '1e-05' -> '1.0e-05', but '1.5e+300' and '6.02e+23' and '1.2345678901234567e+19' pass through untouched.

-0.0 is preserved and emitted as '-0.0'. 0.0 emits '0.0'. Underflowed values emit '0.0' (input 1.0e-324 -> '0.0'). Overflowed values become infinities (input 2.0e+308 -> '.inf', -2.0e+308 -> '-.inf').

INT EMISSION: plain decimal String(value) with no separators, no '+', no leading zeros, arbitrary precision (use BigInt). Integer -0 collapses to '0'. Examples: 1000000000000000000000000000000, 1208925819614629174706176, 9223372036854775808.
BOOL EMISSION: exactly 'true' / 'false' (lowercase). NULL EMISSION: exactly 'null'. All plain, unquoted.
DATE (date-only) EMISSION: 'YYYY-MM-DD' with year zero-padded to 4 digits, month/day to 2. Plain, unquoted. Usable as a mapping key.

DATETIME EMISSION: Python datetime.isoformat(' ') = 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS' (space separator, never 'T'), plus '.ffffff' (exactly 6 digits) ONLY if microsecond != 0, plus the UTC offset as '+HH:MM' / '-HH:MM' ONLY if the value is timezone-aware. Plain, unquoted.

Timezone offsets are NOT converted to UTC and NOT dropped: the offset is stored and re-emitted verbatim (normalized to 2-digit hour and 2-digit minute). '2001-12-14 21:59:43 -5' -> '2001-12-14 21:59:43-05:00'; '...+5:30' -> '...+05:30'; 'Z' -> '+00:00'; '-00:00' -> '+00:00'.

Fractional seconds are TRUNCATED to 6 digits (never rounded) and right-padded with '0' to 6 digits: '.1' -> 100000 us, '.1234567' -> 123456, '.9999999' -> 999999, '.0000001' -> 0 (and therefore omitted on output), '.' (empty fraction) -> 0.

IMPLICIT FLOAT RESOLVER (what makes a scalar a float, YAML 1.1 / PyYAML): /^(?:[-+]?(?:[0-9][0-9_]*)\.[0-9_]*(?:[eE][-+][0-9]+)?|\.[0-9_]+(?:[eE][-+][0-9]+)?|[-+]?[0-9][0-9_]*(?::[0-5]?[0-9])+\.[0-9_]*|[-+]?\.(?:inf|Inf|INF)|\.(?:nan|NaN|NAN))$/ . Key consequences: an exponent MUST carry an explicit '+' or '-' sign; a '.' is mandatory in the mantissa (except for the inf/nan forms); the leading-dot branch '.5' accepts NO sign, so '-.5' and '+.5' are STRINGS.

Float construction from the matched text: strip '_', lowercase; strip a leading '+'/'-' into a sign; '.inf' -> Infinity, '.nan' -> NaN; if it contains ':' treat as sexagesimal (see below); otherwise parseFloat. Signs: '+.inf' -> Infinity, '-.inf' -> -Infinity. '.nan' takes no sign in the implicit form.

SEXAGESIMAL FLOAT: base-60 digits separated by ':', first group /[1-9][0-9_]*/, remaining groups /[0-5]?[0-9]/, and a trailing '.' with optional fraction is required to make it a float. Value = fold(acc*60 + digit). '190:20:30.15' -> 685230.15; '1:20.3' -> 80.3; '1:20.' -> 80.0; '12:00:00.0' -> 43200.0; '1:59:59.999' -> 7199.999.

IMPLICIT INT RESOLVER: /^(?:[-+]?0b[0-1_]+|[-+]?0[0-7_]+|[-+]?(?:0|[1-9][0-9_]*)|[-+]?0x[0-9a-fA-F_]+|[-+]?[1-9][0-9_]*(?::[0-5]?[0-9])+)$/ . Construction: remove all '_'; take sign from leading '-' (default +); drop leading '+'/'-'; if the remainder === '0' return 0; else if it starts with '0b' parse base 2; else if it starts with '0x' parse base 16; else if it starts with '0' parse base 8; else if it contains ':' parse sexagesimal base 60; else parse base 10. Multiply by sign.

IMPLICIT BOOL RESOLVER: only these exact spellings map to booleans — true: yes|Yes|YES|true|True|TRUE|on|On|ON ; false: no|No|NO|false|False|FALSE|off|Off|OFF. Any other casing ('tRue', 'oFf' as an untagged scalar) and the single letters y/Y/n/N are STRINGS.
IMPLICIT NULL RESOLVER: '' (empty scalar), '~', 'null', 'Null', 'NULL'. Other casings ('NuLL', 'nUll') are strings.

IMPLICIT TIMESTAMP RESOLVER: /^(?:[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}|[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{1,2}-[0-9]{1,2}(?:[Tt]|[ \t]+)[0-9]{1,2}:[0-9]{2}:[0-9]{2}(?:\.[0-9]*)?(?:[ \t]*(?:Z|[-+][0-9]{1,2}(?::[0-9]{2})?))?)$/ . Date-only requires exactly 4-2-2 digits (so '2001-1-1' is a string, and '999-01-01'/'10000-01-01' are strings). The datetime branch allows 1-2 digit month/day/hour but REQUIRES 2-digit minute and second (so '2001-1-1 1:2:3' is a string). Separator is 'T', 't', or one-or-more spaces/tabs. 'Z' must be uppercase ('...43z' is a string). Offset minutes, if present, must be exactly 2 digits ('+5:3' -> string).

Note: a literal TAB inside the --a text generally fails earlier in the scanner: yaml.scanner.ScannerError: while scanning for the next token / found character '\t' that cannot start any token (exit code 1), so the tab-separated timestamp form is unreachable at the top level.

Timestamp construction: 4-2-2-only match -> a date object (dumped 'YYYY-MM-DD'); anything with a time part -> a datetime (dumped with the space separator). A datetime at midnight stays a datetime: '2001-12-14 00:00:00' -> '2001-12-14 00:00:00'.

The 76-char base64 wrapping is fixed and is NEVER re-folded to satisfy the emitter's 80-column best_width; at nesting depth 2 lines are 4+76=80 chars, at depth 4 they are 8+76=84 chars. Reproduce it literally.

Round-trip guard (interacts with the string representer): a genuine str whose text WOULD resolve to a non-string must be quoted on output ('1.0', '.inf', 'true', '1', '2001-12-14' -> single-quoted), whereas a str whose text does not resolve (e.g. '1e300', '0o17', '-.5', '.Nan', 'y', 'NuLL', '1:60') is emitted plain and is therefore textually indistinguishable from the input.
surprises: Numbers with exponents but no sign on the exponent are NOT floats in PyYAML's YAML 1.1 resolver: '1e300', '6.02e23', '5e-324', '1e16', '1.7976931348623157e308' all stay strings and echo back unchanged. Only forms like '1.0e+20' / '6.02e+23' become floats. An implementer using a generic YAML 1.2 / JS-Number resolver will parse all of them as numbers and emit different text.
'-.5' and '+.5' are strings while '.5' is the float 0.5 — the leading-dot branch of the float regex has no sign alternative.

Every float gets Python repr formatting, not JS toString: integral floats get a '.0' suffix, the fixed/exponential switch is at 1e16 (not 1e21), and exponents are always signed and zero-padded to 2 digits ('1.0e-05', '1.0e+16'). Additionally PyYAML post-processes repr by inserting '.0' before the first 'e' when the repr has no dot, producing the unusual '1.0e+20' / '5.0e-324' / '1.0e-05' spellings.
-0.0 survives as '-0.0', but integer -0 collapses to '0'.

Sexagesimal (base-60) scalars are real: '1:20' -> 80, '190:20:30.15' -> 685230.15, '60:00' -> 3600. Nearly no other YAML implementation does this, and the validation rules are asymmetric (underscores allowed only in the first group; segments after the first capped at 59; first group must start with 1-9, so '0:0' is a string).
Leading-zero integers are OCTAL ('017' -> 15) but the modern '0o17' prefix is not recognized implicitly (stays a string) — yet under an explicit !!int tag '0o17' DOES parse to 15.
Timezone offsets on timestamps are neither dropped nor normalized to UTC: '2001-12-14 21:59:43.10 -5' round-trips to '2001-12-14 21:59:43.100000-05:00'. But '-00:00' is emitted as '+00:00'.
Fractional seconds are truncated, never rounded: '.1234567' -> '.123456' and '.9999999' -> '.999999'. A fraction that truncates to zero makes the microsecond field disappear entirely from the output.

Date-only timestamps require exactly 4-2-2 digits, but the date+time form accepts 1-2 digit month/day/hour. So '2001-1-1' is a string while '2001-1-1 01:02:03' is a datetime that prints as '2001-01-01 01:02:03'.
'y', 'Y', 'n', 'N' are NOT booleans, but 'on'/'off'/'yes'/'no' are — and only all-lower, Title, or all-upper casings count ('tRue' is a string).
!!binary always wraps base64 at 76 characters and the emitter never re-folds it, so deeply nested binary values produce lines longer than the nominal 80-column width (84 chars at depth 4).

Empty bytes (!!binary "") cannot be a literal block, so it degrades to a double-quoted empty scalar '!!binary ""' — and, because that root scalar is not plain, the '...' document-end line disappears from the output.

All construction failures are uncaught Python tracebacks with exit code 1 and empty stdout, including surprising ones like '2001-12-14 21:59:43+24:00' (offset out of range) and '!!binary "aGVsbG8"' (missing base64 padding). '0000-01-01' also crashes ('year 0 is out of range') rather than resolving to a string.
'!!int ""', '!!float ""', '!!int "-"' fail with IndexError (a raw index-out-of-range on the scalar text), not a YAML error.

surprises: A sequence that is a mapping's value is NOT indented relative to its key — `a:` then `- 1` at column 0. Most YAML emitters indent it. But a sequence that is the value of an EXPLICIT ('? Mapping keys are SORTED, but only best-effort: if any pair of keys is not mutually comparable in Python (e.g. int vs str, None vs str, date vs datetime, bytes vs str), the sort raises TypeError, PyYAML swallows it, and that one mapping is emitted in insertion order. No error is reported. So {1: a, b: c} silently keeps source order while its sibling mappings stay sorted.

The explicit-key '?' threshold is 122/123 RAW characters, not 128, because PyYAML adds the length of the resolved tag ('!!str' = 5) to the key length before comparing to 128. It also uses the raw value length, so a 122-char string that prints as 124 characters of single-quoted text still stays a simple key.

A key can be forced to explicit '? ' form even when it renders on a single line: any string containing a line break (e.g. "a\tb\nc", which prints as "a\tb\nc" double-quoted on one line) is treated as multiline and gets '? ' / ': '.

Collection keys are simply unreachable through safe_load — '{? [1,2]: v}' dies with ConstructorError 'found unhashable key' before dumping. So the '?' indicator in practice only ever precedes a scalar.

!!omap and !!pairs are not round-trippable: they load as a Python list of tuples and dump as an untagged nested block sequence (`- - key` / `  - value`), losing the !!omap tag entirely and skipping sorting. An empty !!omap dumps as `[]`.

!!set survives with its tag, but the tag is emitted on its own line above the entries (`!!set\na: null`), and its element order is NONDETERMINISTIC between runs whenever the elements aren't mutually comparable (Python set iteration order + hash randomization). The same input can produce different bytes on different invocations.

A lone `...` line is appended only for root scalars that end up in PLAIN style. `5` gives "5
...
", but `""` gives "''

All `.nan` scalars share a single cached Python float object, so duplicate NaN keys collapse into one entry ({.nan: 1, .nan: 2} -> ".nan: 2") — the opposite of normal IEEE NaN != NaN behavior. Python dict identity leaks through: `true` and `1` are the same key, and `1.0` and `1` are the same key, so {1: a, true: c} emits a single `1: c` — the key keeps the FIRST inserted object's type but the LAST value.

Stacked block-sequence indicators are never wrapped: 50 nested single-element lists produce one 101-character line, ignoring the 80-column width. Long simple keys are likewise never folded, while long values are.

For index>0: ':' -> block_indicators=True only when followed by whitespace/EOS; '#' -> block_indicators=True only when preceded by whitespace (space, tab, or a break). Characters , ? [ ] { } at index>0 only set flow_indicators, which is irrelevant here because output is always block context.

If space_break or special_characters -> allow_block_plain=False and allow_single_quoted=False. If break_space -> allow_block_plain=False and allow_single_quoted=False. If line_breaks -> allow_block_plain=False. If block_indicators -> allow_block_plain=False. NET EFFECT SUMMARY: DOUBLE-QUOTED is chosen exactly when the string contains any char outside [\x20-\x7E] other than '\n' (so: tab, CR, NUL, any control, DEL, any char >= \x80 including \xa0/ /﻿/emoji), OR contains ' ' immediately before a break, OR contains a break immediately before ' '. SINGLE-QUOTED is chosen for everything else that cannot be plain (leading/trailing space, any newline, leading indicator char, ': ' or trailing ':', ' #', leading '---'/'...', or resolver collision). Otherwise PLAIN.

PLAIN EMISSION: write the raw string. Line folding: scan the string; whenever a run of spaces of length exactly 1 ends and the current output column is > 80, replace that single space with a line break plus the continuation indent; runs of 2+ spaces are never folded. The continuation indent equals (the column at which the key or '- ' item content starts) + 2 — e.g. 2 for a top-level mapping value or root scalar, 4 for a value one level deeper, etc. Plain scalars never contain a newline by construction.

SINGLE-QUOTED EMISSION: write ' then the content with every ' doubled to '', then '. Break runs: a run of N consecutive break chars is written as N+1 physical line breaks followed by the continuation indent (i.e. one

<indent>"; two

<indent>"). Blank lines produced this way carry NO trailing whitespace. Space folding: when a run of exactly one space ends, and the run does not start at offset 0, and the run does not end at the end of the string, and the current output column is > 80, emit a line break + continuation indent instead of the space. Column counting uses the emitted characters (so doubled '' count as 2).

DOUBLE-QUOTED EMISSION: write " ... ". A character is escaped iff it is '"', '\\', \x85,  ,  , ﻿, or is outside \x20-\x7E. Escape table (checked first): \0 -> \0, \x07 -> \a, \x08 -> \b, \x09 -> \t, \x0A -> \n, \x0B -> \v, \x0C -> \f, \x0D -> \r, \x1B -> \e, '"' -> \", '\\' -> \\, \x85 -> \N, \xA0 -> \_,   -> \L,   -> \P. Otherwise: codepoint <= 0xFF -> \xHH; <= 0xFFFF -> \uHHHH; else -> \UHHHHHHHH. Hex digits are UPPERCASE, zero-padded to 2/4/8. Space, '/', "'" are NOT escaped.

DOUBLE-QUOTED FOLDING: while scanning, at index i (strictly 0 < i < len-1), if the current char is a space OR we have just flushed/emitted an escape at this position, and (current column + length of the pending unflushed plain chunk) > 80, then emit the pending chunk followed by a '\\' character, then a line break + continuation indent; if the next character to be emitted is a space, emit an extra '\\' immediately after the indent (so the line resumes with "\\ "). A long run of ordinary printable non-space characters is never folded (there is no flush point).

NON-STRING RENDERING (all plain, unquoted): int -> Python decimal repr (0x1F->31, 0b101->5, 007->7, 1:20->80, -0->0, 685_230->685230). float -> Python repr with these overrides: infinity -> .inf / -.inf, NaN -> .nan; otherwise repr(f) e.g. 0.5, 5.0, 1000.0. bool -> true / false. None -> null. datetime.date -> ISO 'YYYY-MM-DD'; datetime.datetime -> str(dt) i.e. 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS[.ffffff][+HH:MM]' (space separator, microseconds zero-padded to 6, offset as +HH:MM). bytes -> '!!binary |' followed by base64 on indented lines. A set loaded via !!set -> '!!set' tag then mapping entries with null values.

MAPPING KEYS: a key is written inline ("key: value") only if it is a simple key: not empty, not multiline, and len(key_string) + 5 < 128 (the +5 is the length of the implicit tag shorthand '!!str'/'!!int'/etc.), i.e. plain string keys up to 122 chars are inline and 123+ chars become explicit. Non-simple keys are written as '? <key>' on its own line, then ': <value>' on the next line. In simple-key context an empty or multiline scalar is disallowed as plain, and a multiline scalar is disallowed as single-quoted — but since such keys become explicit keys, the simple-key restriction no longer applies and they end up single-quoted.

A Python traceback is printed to stderr followed by '[PYI-<pid>:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test16' due to unhandled exception!', stdout is empty, exit code 1.

allow_unicode is False, so ALL non-ASCII is escaped: é -> \xE9, 中 -> 中, emoji -> \U0001F600 (one 8-digit escape for the astral codepoint, not surrogate pairs). Hex digits are uppercase but the 'x'/'u'/'U' prefix letters keep their case.

result.category: yaml-load: single-quoted and double-quoted flow scalars (escapes, folding, errors)
rules: INPUT MODEL / INTERNAL REPRESENTATION: model the scalar value as an ARRAY OF CODE POINTS, not a JS UTF-16 string. Escapes such as \uD800 produce one code point 0xD800 that must NEVER pair with an adjacent 0xDC00 produced by another escape. (Verified: input "𐀀" dumps as "𐀀", not "\U00010000".) A raw astral char in the input is ONE code point and dumps as \U0001XXXX.

STAGE 0 (reader, runs over the ENTIRE input BEFORE any tokenizing): every code point must be in the printable set {U+0009, U+000A, U+000D, U+0020..U+007E, U+0085, U+00A0..U+D7FF, U+E000..U+FFFD, U+10000..U+10FFFF}. The first violating code point raises `yaml.reader.ReaderError: unacceptable character #x%04x: special characters are not allowed\n  in "<unicode string>", position N` where the hex is LOWERCASE, zero-padded to at least 4 digits, and N is the 0-BASED code point index. This check takes precedence over every scanner/parser error (e.g. `"abc` + 0x01 yields ReaderError, not the unterminated-quote error). Note U+007F..U+0084 and U+0086..U+009F are rejected, but U+0085 is allowed.

SINGLE-QUOTED SCALAR: starts at `'`, ends at the first `'` that is not doubled. `''` inside the scalar yields one literal `'`. No other escape processing whatsoever: backslash, \n, etc. are literal characters. `''''` -> value `'`. Reaching end of input without a closing quote is an error (see UNTERMINATED rule).
DOUBLE-QUOTED SCALAR: starts at `"`, ends at the first `"` not preceded by an (unescaped) backslash. Backslash introduces an escape.

ESCAPE TABLE (double-quoted only). Single-character escapes map as: `0`->U+0000, `a`->U+0007, `b`->U+0008, `t`->U+0009, a LITERAL TAB character (0x09) right after the backslash ->U+0009 (PyYAML extension, not standard YAML), `n`->U+000A, `v`->U+000B, `f`->U+000C, `r`->U+000D, `e`->U+001B, SPACE->U+0020, `"`->U+0022, `/`->U+002F, `\`->U+005C, `N`->U+0085, `_`->U+00A0, `L`->U+2028, `P`->U+2029.

HEX ESCAPES: `x` takes exactly 2 hex digits, `u` exactly 4, `U` exactly 8. Hex digits may be upper or lower case (\ud800 == \uD800). The resulting code point is chr(value). If the value exceeds 0x10FFFF the program dies with a bare `ValueError: chr() arg not in range(0x110000)` (no yaml. prefix, no source-mark info), rc=1. Values in the surrogate range D800..DFFF are ACCEPTED and preserved as lone surrogate code points.

LINE CONTINUATION: a backslash immediately followed by a line break (LF, CR, CRLF, U+0085, U+2028 or U+2029) consumes that break and then, per the BREAK LOOP rule, all spaces/tabs at the start of the following line; it contributes NOTHING to the value. So "a\<LF>b" == "ab". Note the asymmetry: an UNESCAPED U+2028/U+2029 is kept literally, but an ESCAPED one disappears.

UNKNOWN ESCAPE: any other character after the backslash raises `yaml.scanner.ScannerError` with context `while scanning a double-quoted scalar` at the opening quote's mark and problem `found unknown escape character %r` at the mark of the offending character (1-based column). %r is Python repr: normally 'q'-style single quotes, but a single-quote char is rendered as "'". Notable: `\X`, `\'`, `\c`, `\1`..`\9` are all unknown escapes.

BAD HEX ESCAPE: while reading the k required hex digits, the first non-hex-digit character c raises `yaml.scanner.ScannerError`, context `while scanning a double-quoted scalar` at the opening quote, problem `expected escape sequence of %d hexadecimal numbers, but found %r` where %d is 2/4/8 and %r is repr(c). The problem MARK is the position of the FIRST hex digit slot (i.e. immediately after the x/u/U), NOT the position of the offending character.

WHITESPACE/BREAK FOLDING (identical for single- and double-quoted). Scan a run of spaces and tabs. (a) If the run is followed by a NON-break character, the run is appended VERBATIM. (b) If the run is followed by a line break, the run is DISCARDED and folding applies. (c) If the run is followed by end of input, it is an unterminated-scalar error.

FOLDING DETAIL: let b0 be the first break. Normalize CRLF, CR, LF and U+0085 all to U+000A; U+2028 and U+2029 are returned AS THEMSELVES. Then run the BREAK LOOP to collect any further breaks. If b0 normalized is not U+000A (i.e. it was LS or PS) append b0 literally, then append the collected breaks. Else if the collected list is EMPTY append a single SPACE (U+0020). Else append the collected breaks (and no space). Consequence: n consecutive raw breaks produce n-1 literal newlines (1 break -> one space; 2 breaks / 1 blank line -> one \n; 3 breaks -> two \n).

BREAK LOOP (also entered right after a line continuation): repeat { if the current position is at column 0 and the next 3 characters are `---` or `...` AND the 4th is end-of-input, space, tab, CR, LF, U+0085, U+2028 or U+2029, raise the document-separator error; skip all spaces and tabs; if the next character is a break, normalize/consume it and append it to the collected list (LS/PS append themselves, everything else appends U+000A) and continue; otherwise stop }. This is why leading indentation of every continuation line is stripped and why a line containing only spaces/tabs still counts as a blank line.
NO INDENTATION REQUIREMENT: PyYAML deliberately does not check block indentation inside quoted scalars, only the document-separator condition. `k: "a<LF>b"` with `b` at column 0 loads as `k: a b`.

DOCUMENT SEPARATOR ERROR: `yaml.scanner.ScannerError` with context `while scanning a quoted scalar` (note: NOT 'double-quoted') at the opening quote's mark, and problem `found unexpected document separator` at line L column 1 of the offending line. Only column 0 is checked, so an indented `---` and `----` and `---x` are all fine, but `---` followed by space/tab/break/EOF is an error even if the closing quote is on that line after a space.

UNTERMINATED SCALAR ERROR: reaching end of input while the scalar is open raises `yaml.scanner.ScannerError` with context `while scanning a quoted scalar` at the opening quote's mark and problem `found unexpected end of stream` at the mark one past the last character. This covers `"abc`, `'abc`, `"`, `'`, `'''`, and `"abc\"` (the backslash escapes what looked like the closing quote).

TAG RESOLUTION: a quoted scalar is ALWAYS tag:yaml.org,2002:str. No implicit typing. "123", "true", "null", "~", "1.5", "2001-12-14", "" all become strings. Empty `''` and `""` both produce the empty string.

TRAILING CONTENT: a second top-level node after the quoted scalar raises `yaml.parser.ParserError: expected '<document start>', but found '<scalar>'` with a single mark. This happens for `"a"b`, `"a" b`, and `'a'b'`. Trailing spaces or a `# comment` after the closing quote are fine.

ERROR OUTPUT SHAPE (all error cases): stdout is EMPTY, exit code is 1, and stderr contains a Python traceback whose header is `Traceback (most recent call last):` / `  File "test16.py", line 8, in <module>` / the source line, then frames inside yaml/*.py, then the exception line `<ExceptionClass>: <message>`, then a final line `[PYI-<pid>:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test16' due to unhandled exception!`. Marked yaml errors render as: `<class>: <context>
  in "<unicode string>", line L, column C:
    <source line text>
    <spaces>^
<problem>
  in "<unicode string>", line L2, column C2:
    <source line text>
    <spaces>^`. Lines and columns are 1-based; the snippet is indented 4 spaces and the caret sits at 4+(C-1) spaces.

DUMP OF THE LOADED STRING (needed to produce stdout). Three styles: PLAIN, SINGLE-QUOTED, DOUBLE-QUOTED. Only when the emitted style is PLAIN and the value is the whole document does the output end with the explicit document-end marker: `<plain>
...
`. Quoted output is just `<quoted>
`. The program's print() then appends one more `
`. So plain -> "VALUE
...

"; quoted -> "QUOTED

".

DUMP STYLE SELECTION: (1) If the value contains any code point outside U+0020..U+007E other than U+000A (i.e. any control char, TAB, U+0085, U+2028, U+2029, or any non-ASCII), DOUBLE-QUOTED is forced. (2) Otherwise, if a SPACE is immediately followed by U+000A, or U+000A is immediately followed by a SPACE, DOUBLE-QUOTED is forced. surprises: 𐀀 written as two \u escapes does NOT combine into U+10000. It stays two lone surrogates and re-dumps as "𐀀". A naive JS implementation using ordinary JS strings will silently merge them and emit "\U00010000". You must track code points independently.
A lone surrogate escape (\uD800) is accepted without error and round-trips, even though it is not valid Unicode text.
A backslash followed by a LITERAL TAB character (0x09) is a valid escape meaning TAB. This is a PyYAML-only extension and is not in the YAML spec's escape table.
\/ (escaped forward slash) IS accepted (yields /), but \' is NOT (unknown escape character "'").

U+2028 (LS) and U+2029 (PS) are treated as line-break tokens for whitespace-stripping purposes but are NOT folded to a space and NOT normalized to \n -- they are inserted literally. Yet when they follow a backslash they act as line continuations and vanish. U+0085 (NEL) behaves the opposite way: it IS normalized to \n and folded to a space.
U+0085 is a legal input character but U+0086..U+009F and U+007F..U+0084 are not; U+FFFE/U+FFFF are rejected as raw input yet perfectly legal via ￿ escape.
The reader's printability check scans the ENTIRE input before tokenizing, so a stray control character produces a ReaderError even when there is also an unterminated quote earlier/later.
The unterminated-quote and document-separator errors use the context string "while scanning a quoted scalar", while escape errors use "while scanning a double-quoted scalar".

For a bad hex escape the reported mark points at the first hex-digit slot (right after x/u/U) while the reported character is the first non-hex character found -- they are usually different positions.
\U with a value above 0x10FFFF is not a YAML error at all: it escapes as a raw Python ValueError ("chr() arg not in range(0x110000)") with no line/column info.

A quoted multi-line scalar has NO indentation requirement in PyYAML: continuation lines may start at column 0 even inside a mapping. The only positional restriction is that a line must not begin with `---` or `...` followed by whitespace/EOF.
